<reason>Side A won by establishing a decisive test—whether populism leaves citizens able to correct the corrector—and showing populism usually fails it by closing institutional exits and pre-delegitimizing referees. Side B effectively argued populism responds to real elite capture, but struggled to show populism is usually a healthy corrective rather than a warning, as their success examples (Southern Europe) involved movements ceasing to be populist, and their "most stay constitutional" claim was undercut by A's point about opposition-level delegitimization. A's pressure questions exposed contradictions in B's normalization and certification arguments, and A's rebuttals provided the stronger comparative weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (A1 and A2), which argued that backsliding occurs not just through dismantling checks but through pre-delegitimizing referees in opposition, and that populist capture closes plural exits that competitive elite rotation preserves, decisively answering B's baseline-comparison pressure.</best_rebuttal>
